Finding Troy, Damaging Troy: Heinrich Schliemann and the Cost of Discovery

Heinrich Schliemann (1822–1890 CE) is remembered as the man who discovered Troy by following clues in Homer’s Iliad. This description is partly accurate, but it leaves out the help he received and the damage caused by his search. Schliemann showed that Hisarlik contained several ancient settlements. Yet he also rushed through archaeological layers, assigned famous names to objects without enough evidence, and removed artifacts against Ottoman law. His career shows that a major discovery can result from methods that deserve criticism.

Schliemann was born in Neubukow in the Grand Duchy of Mecklenburg-Schwerin. He was not a trained archaeologist. He learned several languages and became wealthy through international trade during the Crimean War. After gaining financial independence, he turned toward Homer and places associated with the Iliad and Odyssey. He later claimed that finding Troy had been his childhood dream, although David Traill argues that this story was probably shaped after Schliemann became famous (Traill, “Dream” 13–24). His wealth allowed him to finance his own excavations.

The popular story also gives Schliemann too much credit for locating Troy. Frank Calvert (1828–1908 CE), a British expatriate who had lived in the Troad for years, had already studied Hisarlik and owned part of the mound. Calvert helped convince Schliemann that Hisarlik was a better candidate than Bunarbashi (Allen). Schliemann supplied money and workers, but Calvert supplied local knowledge. The identification of Troy was therefore a shared achievement, even though Schliemann became its public face.

Schliemann began illegal digging at Hisarlik in 1870 CE and received official permission for later work. He uncovered walls, pottery, and tools. Sebastiani explains that Troy’s position near the Dardanelles made it important for trade between the Aegean, the Black Sea, Europe, and Asia. The discovery therefore mattered for more than Homer. It helped establish Aegean prehistory (Sebastiani; Easton 335–37). It did not prove that every event in the Iliad was historical, but it showed that the poem may have preserved memories of a real place.

The problems became clearer as Schliemann dug deeper. Sebastiani contrasts his methods with modern archaeology, which records layers, contexts, and objects. Schliemann assumed that Homer’s Troy must be near the bottom of the mound, so his workers cut a wide trench through later remains and sometimes used dynamite against obstacles (Sebastiani). This destroyed buildings and stratigraphic evidence. He identified Troy II, an Early Bronze Age settlement, as Priam’s city. Later research showed that Troy II was too early and placed the strongest candidates for Homeric Troy in Troy VI or Troy VIIa. Calvert recognized the dating problem, and Wilhelm Dörpfeld (1853–1940 CE) later helped correct the sequence (Easton 337–39).

Schliemann’s treatment of “Priam’s Treasure” creates a serious cultural heritage issue. He presented its gold, silver, bronze, and copper objects as one discovery connected to King Priam, although Traill argues that the collection included objects found at different times (Traill, “Priam’s Treasure” 17–18). The artifacts belonged to Troy II and were too early for the traditional Trojan War. Schliemann secretly moved the treasure from Ottoman territory to Greece, violating his excavation agreement. Sebastiani also notes that Schliemann displayed ancient jewelry on his wife and treated excavated objects as personal trophies. These actions placed fame and ownership above preservation, law, and respect for cultural heritage.

This balance between achievement and destruction makes Schliemann especially useful for understanding why archaeological ethics developed alongside more careful scientific excavation practices and legal protections for artifacts.

Schliemann deserves recognition for bringing Troy and the Bronze Age Aegean into scholarly attention. However, the heroic version of his life hides too much. Calvert helped lead him to Hisarlik, later archaeologists corrected his dating, and his excavation destroyed evidence that could never be replaced. Troy was rediscovered, but parts of its history were lost during the search. This contradiction explains why modern archaeology values careful recording, legal excavation, scientific methods, and responsibility toward cultural heritage.
